papers.title_in_file: 38 Qiskit, PennyLane QML/QiML Demos - Thanksgiving Eve
papers.what_it_is: A 47-slide seminar deck (Discussion #110, 22 November 2023) in which a company CEO modifies 38 public Qiskit and PennyLane QML tutorials and reports one-run outcomes of each change.

assertions.value: The deck covers 38 demos: Qiskit demos 1 to 12 and PennyLane demos 13 to 38, each revisited with a modification.
quotes: Figure 1: Qiskit (1-12) / PennyLane (13-38) QML/QiML Demos Revisited
assertions.certainty_reason: The deck states its own scope on its first slide.
assertions.reader_inference: The deck is a set of single-configuration demo runs, not a controlled study.

assertions.value: Each demo slide follows one pattern: a stated purpose, a plan, and an action, where the action changes one setting of the tutorial and reports the resulting figure beside the tutorial figure. A short 'New Study' line names a follow-up.
quotes: A) Purpose: Investigate QNN trainable weights, for later finding hidden patterns in data B) Plan: Determine a quantum circuit that changes the weight gradients C) Action: Adding a parametrized Rx gate updated the EstimatorQNN weight gradients
assertions.certainty_reason: The slide format states the paper's own method on slide 2 and repeats it.
assertions.reader_inference: No seeds, repeat counts, variance or significance tests are given anywhere in the text, so each reported change is a single observation.

assertions.value: The authors give a developer guide for simulator speed: use adjoint differentiation (preferred) or back propagation; lightning.qubit is faster than default.qubit and still free; lightning.gpu is significantly faster for larger problems, datasets and specific models, and is not free.
quotes: A) Use adjoint differentiation (preferred) or back propagation in models B) Many models can use lightning.qubit, is faster than default.qubit, and still free C) Lightning.gpu is significantly faster for larger problems/datasets, specific models, not free
assertions.certainty_reason: Practical advice drawn from the author's own demo runs; no systematic benchmark is shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The size of the speed gain depends on the demo; the deck's own timings range from 0.5 seconds saved to roughly an eightfold gain.

assertions.value: The authors state a Colab recipe for GPU simulation: A100 or V100 hardware with lightning.gpu, installed with pip install pennylane pennylane-lightning-gpu custatevec-cu11.
quotes: a) Colab: A100/V100 + lightning.gpu + !pip install pennylane pennylane-lightning-gpu custatevec-cu11
assertions.certainty_reason: An installation recipe stated without version numbers, valid for the time of writing.
assertions.reader_inference: Package names and CUDA wheel names change over time; the recipe is dated to November 2023.

assertions.value: The authors list the levers they tried for circuit performance (double or halve the circuit, use symmetry, change qubit count, embedding type, imprimitive type, layers, entanglement pattern, rotation gates, TorchConnector or TorchLayers count) and for optimizer settings (optimizer, learning rate, weight decay, batch size, dataset, dropout, frozen layers, regularization).
quotes: A) Double circuit, halve circuit, use symmetry, double qubits, halve qubits, etc. B) Switch embedding type, imprimitive type, remove layers, add layers, entanglement pattern
A) Change Optimizer, Learning rate, Weight decay B) Increase Batch size, Dataset, Dropout, etc.
assertions.certainty_reason: A list of tuning options with no evidence of their effect beyond the demos.
assertions.reader_inference: The list names knobs to try; it does not say which help.

assertions.value: In the demo (Qiskit Quantum Neural Networks), the authors report that adding a parametrized Rx gate changed the EstimatorQNN weight gradients from 0.63272767 (tutorial circuit) to 0.89311351 (modified circuit); a follow-up reports 0.4045335.
quotes: Weight gradients 0.63272767
Weight gradients 0.89311351
Weight gradients 0.4045335
Action: Adding a parametrized Rx gate updated the EstimatorQNN weight gradients
assertions.certainty_reason: One run of one tutorial circuit; the text does not say what the weight gradient figure measures.
assertions.reader_inference: A larger gradient value is not shown to give better training.

assertions.value: In the demo (Qiskit Neural Network Classifier and Regressor), the authors report that reducing the ZZFeatureMap repetitions raised the classifier score from 0.8 to 0.85, a 5% increase.
quotes: Classifier score: 0.8
Classifier score: 0.85
Reducing the ZZFeatureMap repetitions increased the classifier score by 5%
assertions.certainty_reason: A single run on a small binary dataset; no repeat or seed information.
assertions.reader_inference: On a small test set a 0.05 change can be one or two samples.

assertions.value: In the demo (training a quantum model on a real dataset), the authors report that increasing the number of EfficientSU2 repetitions from 3 to 4 improved the test score for a Variational Quantum Classifier on data with 2 features. The slide gives no test-score figure in the text layer.
quotes: Use a Variational Quantum Classifier for data with 2 features
Increasing the number of EfficientSU2 repetitions from 3 to 4 improved the test score
assertions.certainty_reason: Single run; the reference list titles the two notebooks '79% Test' and '82% Test' but the slide text carries no score.
assertions.reader_inference: The notebook titles in the works-cited list suggest a rise from 79% to 82% test accuracy, but the slide text does not state it.

assertions.value: In the demo (Qiskit quantum kernel machine learning, spectral clustering), the authors report that changing the ZZFeatureMap entanglement from linear to full raised the clustering score from 0.73 to 1.0.
quotes: ZZFeatureMap entanglement from “linear” to “full” improved results from 0.73 to 1.0
Improve the performance of the Clustering with the Spectral Clustering Model
assertions.certainty_reason: A single run on the tutorial's small dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The tutorial dataset is a small synthetic set; a perfect clustering score may not transfer.

assertions.value: In the demo (PyTorch qGAN), the authors report that shots = 10000 and shots = 1000 yielded comparable differences between CDFs, with the aim of reducing quantum simulator resources.

assertions.reader_inference: The follow-up line says a lower learning rate gave lower final entropy, but the text gives no value.

Test Loss: -7.04

Accuracy: 100.0%
150 images Test Loss: -7.51 Accuracy: 100.0%

assertions.value: In the demo (Pegasos QSVC), the authors report that halving the number of tau steps reduced the runtime by 11.5%, about 3 seconds (25.39 seconds to 22.46 seconds), with the test score unchanged at 1.0. With 2X data the runtime was 16.62 seconds.

PegasosQSVC Test score: 1.0 Runtime

22.46 seconds

assertions.certainty_reason: Single timing runs; wall-clock time is machine and load dependent.
assertions.reader_inference: The 2X data run being faster than a run on half the data suggests timing noise or a changed setting that the slide does not describe.

assertions.value: In the demo (Qiskit quantum kernel training), the authors report that reducing the SPSA optimizer learning rate to 0.048 improved the shape of the loss curve and gave lower losses, with test accuracy 1.0 both before and after.

assertions.value: In the demo (effective dimension of Qiskit neural networks), the authors report that substituting ZFeatureMap for ZZFeatureMap yielded higher normalized global and local effective dimensions. The slide text gives no effective dimension figure; the plots carry them.
quotes: Substituting ZFeatureMap for ZZFeatureMap yielded higher Normalized GLOBAL and
Increase GLOBAL and LOCAL effective dimension capacity measures
assertions.certainty_reason: One comparison seen in plots; no figure in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The reference titles of the follow-up notebooks (10a1 to 10a6) list local values .945 to .985, which the slide text does not explain.

assertions.value: In the demo (Qiskit quantum convolutional neural network), the authors report that doubling the convolutional layer and increasing iterations to 275 lowered objective function values and gave 100% train and 100% test accuracy, against 94.29% train and 73.33% test for the tutorial circuit.

Train Data Acc.: 94.29%, Test Data Acc.: 73.33%
assertions.certainty_reason: Single run on the tutorial's small image set; two changes (layer count and iterations) were made together.
assertions.reader_inference: Because the layer and the iteration count changed together, the slide does not separate their effects.

assertions.value: In the demo (Qiskit quantum autoencoder), the authors report that reducing the RealAmplitudes ansatz from 5 to 3 repetitions lowered runtime by 10.8% (about 4 seconds; 36.48 seconds to 32.55 seconds), improved fidelity of output state with input state from 0.9939 to 0.9997, and let the cost function converge in 50 fewer iterations. A further modified code run shows fidelity 0.99999.
quotes: Reducing the RealAmplitudes ansatz from 5 to 3 repetitions lowered runtime by 10.8% apx. 4 seconds
Fit in 36.48 seconds
Fit in 32.55 seconds
Fidelity of Output State with Input State: 0.9939
Fidelity of Output State with Input State: 0.9997
converged in 50 less iterations
Fidelity of Output State with Input State: 0.99999
assertions.certainty_reason: Single runs; the 0.99999 figure comes from a further change (rhobeg) that the slide only names as a follow-up.
assertions.reader_inference: A shallower ansatz scoring higher on a small state-reconstruction task is plausible, but the slide does not show a repeat.

assertions.value: In the demo (equivariant graph embedding, 5-qubit circuit), the authors report that adding diff_method="adjoint" to the qnode decorator decreased run time from 1.98 seconds to 1.61 seconds, a reduction of 0.37 seconds. A follow-up on an A100 GPU gave 1.21 seconds.
quotes: Time = 1.98 seconds
Time = 1.61 seconds
Adjoint differentiation in qnode decorator decreased model run time by 0.37s
A100 GPU 5 Qubit 1.21s Runtime
assertions.certainty_reason: Single timing runs of under two seconds.
assertions.reader_inference: At this circuit size a difference of 0.37 seconds is within the range of ordinary timing noise.

assertions.value: In the demo (quantum detection of time series anomalies, Quantum Variational Rewinding), the authors report that doubling the number of qubits improved the random models' accuracies prior to training. Covalent, PennyLane and PyTorch were all used.
quotes: Doubling the number of qubits improved random models prior to training
Covalent, Pennylane and PyTorch were all utilized
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison shown in plots; no accuracy figure in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The reference titles read '55% RM1' and 'RY 70% RM1'; the slide text does not state them.

assertions.value: In the demo (introduction to geometric QML, nine qubits representing squares on a board), the authors report that doubling the quantum circuit entangling layer reduced the optimization steps needed and improved validation accuracy for the Standard method.
quotes: Doubling quantum circuit entangling layer reduced optimization steps needed and improved validation accuracy for the Standard method
Nine qubits representings squares on a board.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single comparison shown in plots; no accuracy figure in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The slide does not say whether the symmetric method gained or lost from the same doubling.

assertions.value: In the demo (generalization in QML from few training data), the authors report that accuracies were higher for lower training set sizes N when removing Ising layers, and that a follow-up with a larger circuit improved accuracies at N>5. They note the original authors used 80 samples and reached accuracy greater than 97%.
quotes: Accuracies higher for lower training set sizes N when removing Ising Layers
Authors: 80 samples, accuracy greater than 97%.
Improved Accuracies at N>5 w/ larger circuit
assertions.certainty_reason: Comparisons shown in plots; the text gives no accuracy values for the modification.
assertions.reader_inference: The slide adds that generalization can be seen as a bias-variance trade-off, which is a framing from the tutorial and not a result of the modification.

assertions.value: In the demo (function fitting using quantum signal processing), the authors report that changing qml.RZ(angle) to qml.RZ(angle+0.1) lowered the loss at iteration 16000 from 0.5127 to 0.2863.
quotes: qml.RZ(angle, wires=0) iter: 16000, loss: 0.5127
qml.RZ(angle+0.1, wires=0) iter: 16000, loss: 0.2863
Modifying angle parameter to angle+0.1 resulted in a large reduction in Loss at
assertions.certainty_reason: One run each; the shift is a hand-picked offset with no explanation of why it helps.
assertions.reader_inference: A shift of the phase angle changes the fitted polynomial, so a lower loss may come from a different initialization and not from a better method.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Singular Value Transform (QSVT) is fundamental to algorithms like Shor's factoring algorithm and Grover search, and that QSVT applies polynomial transformations to the singular values of any matrix.
quotes: Quantum Singular Value Transform (QSVT) is fundamental to algorithms like Shor’s factoring algorithm, and Grover search
QSVT applies polynomial transformations to the singular values of any matrix
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement taken from the PennyLane tutorial, with no proof in the deck.
assertions.reader_inference: QSVT unifies Grover search and Shor's algorithm in the framework literature, but the deck gives no source and no conditions.

assertions.value: In the demo (machine learning for quantum many-body problems, classical shadows), the authors report that switching from default.qubit to lightning.qubit reduced runtime from 233.54 seconds to 208.08 seconds, a saving of 25.5 seconds.
quotes: qml.device("default.qubit", wires=num_qubits) Time = 233.54 seconds
qml.device("lightning.qubit", wires=num_qubits) Time = 208.08 seconds
Switching from default.qubit to lightning.qubit reduced runtime by 25.5 seconds
assertions.certainty_reason: Single wall-clock runs on one machine.
assertions.reader_inference: 233.54 minus 208.08 is 25.46 seconds, consistent with the stated 25.5 seconds, a gain of about 11%.

assertions.value: In the demo (quantum advantage in learning from experiments), the authors report runtimes of 27.52 seconds on a Colab A100 with lightning.gpu, 35.17 seconds on a Colab V100 with lightning.gpu, and 197.77 seconds on Colab CPU with default.qubit. They also report that decreasing ratio_imprim decreased entangling gates and improved class separations for the 'without quantum memory' model.
quotes: Time = 27.52s Colab A100 Lightning.gpu
Time = 35.17s Colab V100 Lightning.gpu
Time = 197.77s Colab CPU Default.qubit
Decreasing ratio_imprim decreased entangling gates and improved class
assertions.certainty_reason: Single timing runs on Colab hardware; the class separation result is read from plots.
assertions.reader_inference: 197.77 divided by 27.52 is about 7.2, so the A100 run was about seven times faster than the CPU run for this demo only.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing the tutorial, that experiments with quantum memory do not have the limitations of conventional experiments. The purpose of the demo is to determine how useful access to quantum memory is for quantum ML.
quotes: B) Experiments with quantum memory do not have the limitations of conventional experiments
To determine how useful is access to quantum memory for quantum ML
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement restated from the tutorial; the deck does not test it.
assertions.reader_inference: The deck's change to ratio_imprim tests an engineering variable, not this premise.

assertions.value: In the demo (tensor-network quantum circuits), the authors report that a 10-qubit block MPS circuit was constructed following the code in the model, in place of the authors' 4-qubit block MPS, and that a follow-up extends it to 20 qubits. They state that tensor-network quantum circuits emulate the shape and connectivity of tensor networks MPS and TTN.
quotes: 10 Qubit block MPS circuit was constructed following the code in the model
Tensor-network quantum circuits emulate shape, connectivity of tensor networks MPS, TTN
Increase MPS circuit to 20 Qubits, adding color
Authors’ 4 Qubit block MPS
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction shown as a circuit drawing; no performance figure.
assertions.reader_inference: This demo builds a larger circuit and reports no accuracy or runtime.

assertions.value: In the demo (approximating a classical kernel with a quantum computer), the authors report that setting expansion_strategy to 'device' shortened runtime by 0.5 seconds (14.13 seconds to 13.54 seconds, on lightning.qubit). A follow-up increases wires to increase frequencies, noting 2^5 = 32 frequencies and 2^7 = 128 frequencies.
quotes: 14.13 seconds lightning.qubit
13.54 seconds lightning.qubit
Setting expansion_strategy to ‘device” shortened runtime by 0.5 seconds
2^5 = 32 Frequencies
2^7 = 128 Frequencies
assertions.certainty_reason: Single timing runs of about 14 seconds.
assertions.reader_inference: A 0.6 second difference on a 14 second run is a 4% change with no repeat.

assertions.value: In the demo (quantum GANs), the authors report that increasing quantum depth from 6 to 10 decreased the generator loss from 1.061 to 0.644 at iteration 500 (discriminator loss 0.824 and 1.227) and that image quality more closely resembled the actual images.
quotes: q_depth = 6 Iteration: 500, Discriminator Loss: 0.824 Generator Loss: 1.061
q_depth = 10 Iteration: 500, Discriminator Loss: 1.227 Generator Loss: 0.644
By increasing quantum depth from 6 to 10, Generator loss decreased significantly and image quality more closely resemble Actual images
assertions.certainty_reason: One run each; image quality is judged by eye.
assertions.reader_inference: In a GAN a lower generator loss is not by itself a sign of better samples.

assertions.value: In the demo (unitary designs), the authors report that decreasing flip_prob by an order of magnitude raised the mean fidelity from 0.98687 (flip_prob 0.01) to 0.98978 (0.001), with 0.99008 at 0.0001. The Haar-random mean fidelity equals the mean fidelity at each setting, and the Clifford mean fidelity differs in the fifth decimal. They state that only 24 experiments were needed to compute the average fidelity.
quotes: flip_prob = 0.01 Mean fidelity = 0.98687 Haar-random mean fidelity = 0.98687 Clifford mean fidelity = 0.98681
flip_prob = 0.001 Mean fidelity = 0.98978 Haar-random mean fidelity = 0.98978 Clifford mean fidelity = 0.98971
flip_prob = 0.0001 Mean fidelity = 0.99008 Haar-random mean fidelity = 0.99008 Clifford mean fidelity = 0.99006
Only 24 experiments were needed to compute the average fidelity
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated fidelities from a noise-parameter sweep on default.mixed with shots=None; less noise giving higher fidelity is expected.
assertions.reader_inference: Fidelity rising as the bit-flip probability falls is an expected result of the noise model and does not test the unitary design claim itself.

assertions.value: In the demo (training and evaluating quantum kernels), the authors report that substituting CRZ for CNOT gates in the ring pattern gave 100% classification prior to training. They state that the quantum kernel alone cannot be used to make predictions and that scikit-learn's Support Vector Classifier performs the prediction.
quotes: By substituting CRZ for CNOT gates, 100% classification prior to training
The quantum kernel alone can not be used to make predictions on a dataset
To perform an actual prediction: scikit-learn’s Support Vector Classifier (SVC)
assertions.certainty_reason: One run on the tutorial dataset; the second and third quotes restate the tutorial.
assertions.reader_inference: The reference lists a variant named '50% No Train', so the effect of gate choice depends on the dataset or setting; the slide text does not give that detail.

assertions.value: In the demo (understanding the Haar measure), the authors report that adding shifts phi-1 and omega+1 to qml.Rot gave a different distribution of states. They state that one does not always need to sample from the full Haar measure.
quotes: A different distribution was obtained by adding shifts to: phi-1 omega+1
Do not always need to sample from the full Haar measure.
assertions.certainty_reason: A distribution shown in plots; the second quote restates the tutorial.
assertions.reader_inference: Shifting two Euler angles by fixed offsets is not a unitary-invariant change, so the result is no longer Haar random by construction.

assertions.value: In the demo (learning to learn with quantum neural networks, QAOA for MaxCut), the authors report that raising the Adam learning rate from 0.1 to 0.2 for the first 2 Adam instances decreased time from 225.93 seconds to 207.98 seconds with a similar final loss of -1.5948243.
quotes: Adam learning_rate = 0.1 (original Adam instances) 225.93 seconds
Adam learning_rate = 0.2 (first 2 Adam instances) 207.98 seconds
Final Loss = -1.5948243
Increased Adam optimizer learning rate to 0.2 decreases time, similar results
assertions.certainty_reason: Two single runs with wall-clock times; only the first 2 Adam instances changed.
assertions.reader_inference: The time saved is 17.95 seconds, about 8%.

assertions.value: In the demo (kernel-based training of quantum models with scikit-learn), the authors report a runtime of 44.72 seconds on an A100 with lightning.gpu and adjoint differentiation, against 367.29 seconds on CPU with lightning.qubit and parameter-shift. Switching the imprimitive to CZ gave loss 0.406 against 0.420 at step 100, with test accuracy 0.96 in both.
quotes: A100 Lightning.gpu, Adjoint differentiation 44.72s
CPU, Lightning.qubit, parameter-shift 367.29s
step 100 , loss 0.420
step 100 , loss 0.406
accuracy on test set: 0.96
assertions.certainty_reason: Single runs; hardware and gradient method differ together, so the two timings do not isolate either.
assertions.reader_inference: The ratio 367.29 to 44.72 is about 8.2, but it combines a GPU change and a differentiation-method change.

assertions.value: The authors state, from the tutorial, that unless the variational circuit has significantly fewer parameters than training data, kernel methods could be a much faster alternative.
quotes: Unless variational circuit has significantly fewer parameters than training data, kernel methods
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement restated from the PennyLane tutorial; the deck does not test it.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence continues on the next text line ('could be a much faster alternative') in the extracted text.

assertions.value: In the demo (turning quantum nodes into Keras layers), the authors report that 12 layers gave training loss 0.1387 against 0.1423 for 6 layers, with training accuracy 0.8733 and validation accuracy 0.8400 in both. A modified neural network gave validation accuracy 0.8600.

Benchmark runs gave 5.55 s, 4.27 s and 4.10 s (A100), all with 83.2%, and the authors state speed differences are less evident for the smaller Iris dataset.

assertions.value: In the demo (quantum transfer learning), the authors report that removing the entangling layer from the 4-qubit dressed quantum circuit gave a faster time (1m 12s against 1m 20s), lower best test loss (0.4186 against 0.4484) and higher best test accuracy (0.8693 against 0.8497). Increasing circuit depth to 8 raised best test accuracy to 90.9% (0.9085, 5m 8s on CPU).

Training completed in 1m 12s Best test loss: 0.4186 | Best test accuracy: 0.8693
Removing entangling layer yielded faster time, lower loss, higher accuracy
Training completed in 5m 8s (CPU) Best test loss: 0.4360 | Best test accuracy: 0.9085
Increasing circuit depth to 8 increased best test accuracy to 90.9%
Features are then classified by a 4-qubit “dressed quantum circuit”

assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of absence over the whole text layer, resting on the quotes only as examples of untested follow-up ideas.
